content: The document outlines key recommendations and updates from the World Health Organization (WHO) regarding tuberculosis (TB) prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, particularly in children and adolescents. Below is a professional summary of the content: 1. Global Public Health and Vaccination Programs: The WHO provides guidance on the use of vaccines in large-scale national immunization programs. These recommendations are based on systematic evaluations of diseases and vaccines, with input from external experts and the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on immunization. The GRADE methodology is used to assess the quality of available data, and decisions are documented in detailed data tables. 2. Target Audience for WHO Position Papers: These papers are primarily intended for national public health officials and vaccination program administrators. However, they are also relevant to international funding organizations, vaccine manufacturers, healthcare professionals, researchers, scientific media, and the general public. 3. BCG Vaccine Recommendations: The Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, derived from Mycobacterium bovis, is recommended at birth for all healthy neonates in countries with high TB incidence. In low-incidence countries, it may be selectively administered to high-risk groups. Revaccination is not recommended, even if the initial vaccination does not leave a scar. BCG vaccination is contraindicated in individuals with immunodeficiency, including infants exposed to immunosuppressive treatments or born to HIV-positive mothers unless they are clinically stable and on antiretroviral therapy (ART). 4. TB Screening and Diagnosis in Children: Children under 15 years of age, whether living with HIV or not, can be screened for TB using specific signs and symptoms. The absence of these symptoms generally excludes active TB. Diagnostic tools such as Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra are preferred over smear microscopy and culture for detecting TB and rifampicin resistance in children. Specimens like induced sputum, gastric aspirates, nasopharyngeal aspirates, stool, or site-specific samples (e.g., cerebrospinal fluid for TB meningitis) are recommended. Chest radiography and tuberculin skin testing may also aid in diagnosis, especially in cases of suspected pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB. 5. Challenges in Diagnosing Childhood TB: Children with pulmonary TB often do not produce sufficient respiratory secretions for testing, and microbiological confirmation is achieved in less than 30% of cases. Diagnosis may rely on clinical parameters and additional investigations, such as chest X-rays or biopsies. 6. Treatment of TB in Children: TB treatment regimens for children are based on adult drugs but require weight-based dosage adjustments due to faster metabolism in children. Child-friendly fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) are recommended. Infants aged 1–3 months may need dose adjustments to minimize toxicity, under the supervision of a pediatric TB specialist. Children with drug-susceptible TB are treated with a combination of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for four months. For TB meningitis or osteoarticular TB, treatment duration is extended to 12 months. Streptomycin is not recommended as part of first-line treatment regimens for children. 7. Nutritional Support for Children with TB: Malnutrition is a significant risk for children with TB, especially in emergency settings. Nutritional support includes continued breastfeeding (up to 24 months where possible) and ensuring adequate nutrient intake through locally available foods. Infants under six months with malnutrition concerns should be referred to therapeutic feeding programs. 8. Management of TB in Neonates Born to Mothers with TB: Infants born to mothers with active pulmonary TB should be assessed for TB disease and treated if necessary. If asymptomatic, they should receive TB preventive treatment (TPT). BCG vaccination should be delayed until TPT is completed to avoid the risk of disseminated BCG disease. 9. Updates on TB Treatment Guidelines: A shorter four-month treatment regimen is recommended for children aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB. For children with multidrug-resistant (MDR) or rifampicin-resistant (RR) TB, bedaquiline and delamanid are recommended as part of all-oral regimens. A six-month intensive regimen is suggested for children with drug-susceptible TB meningitis as an alternative to the standard 12-month regimen. 10. HIV and TB Co-Infection: Children living with HIV who are receiving TB treatment may require modifications to their antiretroviral therapy (ART) and closer monitoring. Routine HIV testing is recommended for all individuals with presumptive or confirmed TB. 11. Patient-Centered Care: 12. Decentralized and Family-Centered Services: In high TB burden settings, integrated and family-centered services are encouraged to improve TB case detection and uptake of preventive treatment. 13. Monitoring and Adverse Reactions: TB treatment in children requires frequent monitoring to adjust drug dosages based on weight gain and to manage adverse reactions. Serious adverse events are less common in children than in adults, but isoniazid-induced pyridoxine deficiency (manifesting as neuropathy) may occur, particularly in malnourished or HIV-positive children. Pyridoxine supplementation is recommended in such cases. 14. Operational Handbook for TB Management: The upcoming 2022 WHO operational handbook will include integrated treatment decision algorithms for children under 10 years, combining bacteriological testing, chest X-ray findings, and clinical symptoms to guide treatment decisions. 15. TB Prevention in High-Risk Groups: Neonates born to mothers with bacteriologically confirmed TB should receive TPT if TB disease is excluded. These recommendations aim to improve TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment outcomes in children and adolescents, with a focus on evidence-based practices and patient-centered care.
